utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good afternoon to you, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, yes, I can. I can understand as well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please sit down. And good afternoon to you, Madam Richterova, appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Anna Richterova for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good afternoon to you. And Mr. Ackerman, appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, I'm here today with my co-counsel, Milan Trbojevic, and Marela Jevtovic and I'd like to introduce you to Ms. Barbara Baruch, who has now joined our team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, welcome to the Tribunal and good afternoon to you all. So can we start with the witness or is there anything that you like to raise? Nothing? Okay. Do you pronounce it Baruch or Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Baruch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Alkic, and welcome back. I hope you had a nice weekend. Let's proceed straight away with the solemn declaration once more, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, and welcome back.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When we broke on Friday we were talking about what had happened in Kupres in early 1992 or what was happening there and in that connection I'd like you to take a look at another document. I'd like you to look at P885, please. Now, this document, sir, is a military secret, strictly confidential, coded document from the 5th Corps Command to the 2nd Military District Command and it has to do with basically a report on the disposition of the forces of the 30th Partisan division and contains some information which I'd like to go through with you. If you look on what might be the second page, you'll see a paragraph beginning with, "In Bugojno, SJB." Do you find that paragraph? Just let me know when you find the paragraph that begins with the words, "In Bugojno." It's at the end of the first page. Can you not find it or what?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It reads this way: "In Bugojno SJB, public security station, ammunition has been distributed to the wartime police but only to Muslim members who were also told to keep this secret from members of the Croatian nationality." Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, April and early May, I was in Donji Vakuf and I didn't know what was going on in Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But you very soon after that went to Bugojno, did you become familiar with ammunition having been distributed only to Muslim members of the police?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived in Bugojno, police, both Bosniak and Croatian police, had some weaponry and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next paragraph says this: "Relations between Croats and Muslims in Gornji Vakuf are tense." Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: About 200 HOS members were sighted in Turbe, their headquarters located in the Feniks cafe. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I came out in mid-May to the village called Karaula, and Turbe, I know of certain circumstances that existed in the village of Turbe. During that period of time, it couldn't have been 200 members of HOS there in that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any HOS forces in that village?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any HOS forces in the area of Bugojno? Either in Bugojno or in that area?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next paragraph says HOS forces captured --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Ackerman, were you aware at the time of the Feniks cafe serving as the headquarters for HOS members in Turbe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next paragraph says: "HOS forces captured the Koprivnica-Bugojno residence." And I don't know if this is translated properly: "Our forces in the area are weak." Do you know what the Koprivinica-Bugojno residence is?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is it in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is far from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How far?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bit more than 10 kilometres, perhaps 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about that being -- what is it? Is it a building, is it a residence? What is it? What is --

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the old or rather new villa of Josip Broz.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know anything about it having been captured by HOS forces?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part or shall I call it that area was never controlled by the army forces in 1992. Their front was some 6 to 7 kilometres away from Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the question, sir, that I was really trying to get from you is: Do you know anything about that villa being captured by HOS forces?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when you say it was the new villa of Josip Broz, you're referring to Tito, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where is the village of Donji Malovan?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Donji Malovan is to the southwest from Kupres in the direction of Livno, on the very road leading to that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the paragraph says that HOS forces captured the village of Donji Malovan and dispatched ten tanks which are engaged in fighting in the Suica village area. Did you ever observe HOS forces having tanks in their arsenal?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next paragraph -- is Suica village near Donji Malovan?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that I'm not familiar with that area, I do think that it's in the vicinity of Donji Malovan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. "The HOS is holding Kupreska Vrata, blocking the passage to Bugojno." Would that be the tunnel we were talking about that was right on the edge of Kupres?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Two buses with HOS forces set off from Jajce and one set off from Bugojno towards Kupres." Do you know anything about these forces leaving Bugojno and Jajce to go to Kupres?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Strong HOS forces are deployed in Livno and Tomislavgrad, around Kupres the forces are deployed around the villages of Rasticevo, Ravno and Zlosela." Do you know about those HOS forces deployed in those villages around Kupres?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Finally, the report, which is signed by Colonel Tomislav Damjanovic says: "According to our intelligence, there are two ZNG, National Guard Corps brigades in the area and they are constantly gaining in strength." Were you aware of the presence of ZNG brigades or units in the Bugojno-Kupres area?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see any ZNG forces in the area of Bugojno during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next document I'd like you to look at is DB138, please. Now this is another document, sir, from the 5th Corps. It's dated 4 April, 1992, addressed to the command of the 2nd Military District. It's a regular combat report. The last two paragraphs under paragraph number 1 read as follows: "The Kupres area is the main target of attack by Ustasha formations. The main access of the attack is from Suica via Malovan towards Kupres, up to two battalions of a tank company supported by artillery are attacking along that axis." Now, you were certainly aware in early April, 1992, that there was some kind of combat activity going on at Kupres, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you knew that that combat activity was between Croatian and Serbian forces with Muslim forces involved in support of the Croatian forces? You knew that too, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly along those lines. I knew that the conflict between the Serb forces or rather the JNA and the Croatian forces was in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The next paragraph reads: "Columns of Ustasha motor vehicles have been noticed moving from the Gornji Vakuf and Bugojno areas towards Kupres. Ustasha forces the strength of a battalion have dug themselves in, in the area of Rasticevo, Zlosela, and Osmanlije villages. The Ustashas will probably extend the attack with the goal of capturing Kupres and its plateau." In fact, that's what happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a lot of illogical -- there are a lot of illogical things in these two sentences. Whoever wrote this report probably did not use a map, nor did he know where the village of Rasticevo is located, as well as the village of Osmanlije and Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you want to explain that further or not? I'll give you the opportunity to do so, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, and as far as I know, Rasticevo, Zlosela and Osmanlije are the villages located between Janj Plateau and Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how far would they be from Kupres?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know. Probably several kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Several could be as few as five, not more than ten?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to change subject matter now. I'm going to refer now to something you said in your statement of September, 2001. I think it might be useful for the Prosecutor to return that to you at this point. I'm looking at page 3 of the English version where you're talking about the removal of weapons from the TO warehouse to the JNA warehouse, and what you indicate there, in fact I think you say it clearly, yes, you say, "Left the TO warehouse, placed in the JNA Daljan warehouse but I'm not sure of the exact date." I'd like you to look in connection with that at document DB137. This is a document, sir, which appears to have been issued by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, main staff of the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. First administration. It's document number 19-1, dated 14 May, 1990. Now, in 14 May, 1990, Yugoslavia, with all of its republics, still existed, did it not?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it did not. Or rather, yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this is an order, it says deliver immediately to the commander personally and it deals with safekeeping of weapons and ammunition of the TO. And it reads as follows, in part: "In order to provide for the safe storage and safekeeping of the Territorial Defence weapons and ammunition, and in keeping with the tasks laid out by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence at the military council session held on 27 April, 1990, I hereby issue the following order. Number 1, the military district air force and naval district commands, together with the TO staffs of the socialist republics and socialist autonomous provinces," that's everybody, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Alkic, please answer the question. You are being asked whether by referring to the socialist republics and socialist autonomous provinces, this document was addressing the entirety of what was then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: TO units in what was then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It probably did address all of the units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it says that, "all of those units shall organise the takeover, storage and safekeeping of the complete stock of the TO weapons and ammunition in the JNA supply dumps and depots. Within the scope of further organisational and establishment improvements, TO commanders shall consider the possibility of abolishing certain smaller TO units whose weapons and ammunition cannot be safeguarded in the JNA dumps and depots." A little further down, it talks in paragraph 2, "exceptionally, where facilities are very far away and where conditions are not conducive to or it is impossible to find a place for TO weapons and ammunition in JNA depots, they should be stored and safeguarded in TO depots, guarded by JNA units." And then finally, well, not finally, paragraph 3, "The TO staffs and TO units are to take out weapons and ammunition required for the execution of planned activities with the approval of the military district commands. The military district commands shall issue special instructions regulating the entry, maintenance and safekeeping procedures as well as the procedure for taking out and returning weapons and ammunition to the depots." 4, "The collection and storage of weapons and ammunition is to be completed by 21 May, 1990." And then finally, "Submit a report on the execution of this order with the exact breakdown of the quantities and types of ammunition being kept in JNA dumps and depots and exceptionally in the TO depots to the OS main staff first administration by 5 June, 1990." It's signed by the chief of GSOSFRJ, Colonel General Blagoje Adzic. Did you ever hear of General Blagoje Adzic?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This document tells you, does it not, the date upon which this order was entered for the removal of weapons from the TO warehouses and their transport to JNA warehouses, that being 14 May, 1990; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it additionally tells you that this was done throughout former Yugoslavia, in every republic, with regard to every TO, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what happened throughout Yugoslavia but I received an order from the district TO, after which we stored the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where do you suggest that the document, Mr. Ackerman, where do you suggest that this document says that this was done throughout former Yugoslavia and every republic with regard to every TO? Because you seem to be saying that this -- it specifies the order and also specifies that the order was executed, but I see no where in the document such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I may have -- my question may have been poorly worded, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Your question was, and it additionally tells you that this was done throughout former Yugoslavia and every republic with regard to every TO, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This I referred to the order. We will see the result of that order in just a second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the document itself doesn't say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No. The order was issued in every FTO in former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And now, sir, I'd like you to look at P19 and we will see what happened with regard to this order. Now, this document, sir, and I'm only interested in the first page of the document, it's dated 13 September, 1990. It refers to the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it speaks of this order we were just talking about, order number 19-1, of 14 May, 1990. And it says this in the first two paragraphs: "Pursuant to the order of the head of the chiefs of staff of the armed forces of the SFRY, Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, strictly confidential, number 19-1, of 14 May, 1990, the action geared to take over and secure the armaments and ammunition of the ONO, All People's Defence, and DSZ, Social Self-Protection, subjects in the JNA depots, was conducted in the territory of the SFRY. The relocation of the TO Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina armaments and ammunition was carried out between 18 May and 23 May, 1990, with the exception of the region of Bihac and Banja Luka where it was completed on 13 June, 1990." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And so it appears, does it not, that the weapons were removed from every TO within the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and put within the control of the JNA between the 18th of May and the 13th of June of 1990. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Friday, in your testimony, you mentioned that you had discussed this removal of TO weapons to JNA control with Mr. Osman Selak; is that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it -- Mr. Ackerman, sorry to interrupt. Is it the Serbian Republic of BiH or the Socialist Republic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did I say Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly because you have been referring to Serbian Republic of BiH throughout and that's certainly not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not, it's the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's being corrected for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for pointing that out. It was the Bosnia-Herzegovina that existed before the break-up, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The secession.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us, I think, on Friday that you had discussed this with Osman Selak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you refer, please, to the page of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wish I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wish I could, and I can't. I forgot to make the note so I will abandon the question rather than.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said, Mr. Ackerman, if I remember well, you -- someone did ask him whether he knew Osman Selak. And he said that knew of the existence of Osman Selak and that on one occasion, he was at a meeting or somewhere standing next to him, but he was not introduced to Mr. Selak. So he'd never had the opportunity to discuss anything with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: As I went through the transcript, it was in reference to the second transfer of the weapons, not this first one in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But in any case, forget the transfer of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm satisfied to leave it where it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, I want to refer now to page 4 of your statement, and there is a paragraph on page 4 in the English version that begins with the language, "I mentioned in my previous statement that the SDS took political control in Donji Vakuf." And then you go on in that paragraph to talk about attending certain meetings in 1992, that they were organised by the head of the municipality, that they were usually designed to discuss the security situation in Donji Vakuf, and then you ended with this sentence: "The Serbs tried to justify what they were doing by saying that it was to protect the Serb people. I don't recall specifically who said these things." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, it was Colonel or Lieutenant Colonel Kostic who told me that. I asked him about the Daljan barracks and he was the one who told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who told you that they were trying to justify what they were doing by saying that it was protect the Serb people?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from ten other people apart from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah. "And we are in a situation in Donji Vakuf at this point where, within a very few kilometres, there is armed combat going on between the JNA and Croatian forces, we are 12 kilometres away from Bugojno where there are Croat forces who may be in possession of tanks," that was certainly information that was disseminated at that point in time. Don't you think that there was a legitimate basis for fear on the part of the Serb residents of Donji Vakuf and a need to at least take some steps to protect themselves from an attack by the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was the person who was supposed to know what was going on in the area of Kupres in the month of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... person who was supposed to but you told us on Friday that you didn't know, so the person who was supposed to know didn't know, but I think you'll agree that you could hear the sounds of the combat all the way to Donji Vakuf. You could hear the sounds of the weapons, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may continue with my previous answer, in view of the fact that I had to know and in view of the fact that I didn't know that, I claim here with full responsibility that many Serb residents from local -- from Donji Vakuf didn't know about what was going on in Kupres either. The information that people had had mostly come from the explosions and detonations that were coming from the direction of Kupres so they made their conclusions on the basis of that and I am referring to the population of Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I suppose you'd agree that there were at least rumours going around at the time, whether they were correct or not, there were at least rumours going around about what was happening in Kupres?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the information that you got from Kostic, you talked about on page 6 of your statement where you said: "During my conversations with Kostic, he explained to me that he and a group of officers had come to Donji Vakuf to form and organise the Serb people in Donji Vakuf, and justified this by saying that the Serb people in Donji Vakuf were threatened." Is that what you were referring to a moment ago when you said you heard it from him?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where was it he came from when he came to Donji Vakuf? Do you know where he'd been right before that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from Darko Savic that he had retired, that he had been a member of the JNA but that upon an invitation by the SDS and JNA, he became active again but that's all I know about that man. I think he had come from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess you'd have to agree that it's likely that he had valid information about what was going in the area of Kupres when he arrived in Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Back on page 5 of your statement, you make the following assertion: It's a paragraph that begins with, "The SDS." You say: "The SDS in Donji Vakuf before March, 1992, received certain guidelines from higher SDS leaders regarding preparations for war. I say this because the SDS authorities in Donji Vakuf were regularly going to Banja Luka for meetings and that was the conclusion I drew." Now, let's discuss that a bit. You claim to know that SDS authorities in Donji Vakuf were regularly going to Banja Luka for meetings. How is it you know that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from the conversations I had with Serb officials who were employees of the Municipal Assembly. I talked to them every day and they told me accidentally or on purpose, I don't know, that a so and so member of the SDS had gone to Banja Luka for a meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Give me the names of these Serb officials who told you that.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Surutka, Zoran Glisic, Mile Ilic, Novo Zelic, Predrag Vujic. So it was through everyday conversations was these men that I was able to learn that a certain SDS leader was away in Banja Luka. They went there from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then what you say about this, after learning that SDS leaders or a leader were going to Banja Luka for meetings you say, "The conclusion I drew" then go back to the beginning, "Was that they received certain guidelines from higher SDS leaders regarding preparations for war." Now, that's just a kind of guess on your part, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before these activities started, very few party or municipal officials ever went to Banja Luka. They mostly went to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me stop you. My question is simple: The proposition that they went there to receive guidelines from higher SDS leaders regarding preparations for war is a conclusion that you drew based upon your knowledge they were going to Banja Luka. That's my only question. Is that true or not true?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You tell us on page 7 of your statement that you left Donji Vakuf and fled to Bugojno and joined the army. True?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fled to Travnik and from Travnik to Bugojno where I joined the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when was that, that you joined the army?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what --

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it was not until June that I actually joined the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what army was that that you joined?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the TO staff of Bugojno, Bugojno and Donji Vakuf TO staff. They acted jointly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And which became the army of -- part of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There were also other Bosniaks who left Donji Vakuf that joined that army too, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your statement you said -- you said this: This is on page 8. "On the 29th of May, I reported to the Secretariat for People's Defence in Bugojno. After that, I stayed in Bugojno for about ten days and then I went to Gornji Vakuf. I was still in civilian clothes. I stayed in Gornji Vakuf for 20 days and following that I was called to Bugojno to help in organising the Defence of Bugojno. I was engaged in the municipal TO staff in Bugojno for ten to 15 days. After that, the municipal TO staff assigned me to the 1st Battalion in Bugojno as operations officer." That was kind of the sequence of events by which you became a member of that army; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, a little bit above that on the same page, you are talking about the departures from Donji Vakuf, and you refer to it as being disorganised and like a stampede, and that most people went on foot to Bugojno. What was it about Bugojno that made it a safe place, 12 kilometres away from Donji Vakuf that made it a safe place for people to go?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was the closest municipality or the closest town with respect to Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But there was something -- there must have been something else about it that made it safe, like it was in control of Bosniaks or Croats or something; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trust me, while I was in Donji Vakuf, I was not aware of the situation in Bugojno, but I was aware of course of the fact that the JNA forces were not concentrated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, someone must have been aware of it or these large numbers of people would not have left Donji Vakuf and gone to Bugojno if they thought they were going to a more dangerous place; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main reason why we went for Bugojno and why many people went to Croatia was the fact that that was the best route to take, the best communication to take, and that was the closest municipality to Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The fact is that Bugojno was Muslim territory, that there were Muslim and Croat forces deployed in Bugojno, and that people felt safe going there. That's a fair statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can -- could be a fair statement now, yes, but at the time, I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at, it's on page 9 in the English version, of your statement. You talk about in September of 1992 being appointed as the 1st Battalion commander in Bugojno. And then a little further down, you talk about a unit coming from Djurici and you say this: "The unit coming from Djurici was supported by one tank." Now, that would be a JNA-VRS unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's on page 10 of your version, sir, paragraph begins, the unit coming from Djurici. Third paragraph, you got it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The unit coming from Djurici that you refer to would have been a VRS unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say: "It was supported by one tank which was rolling along the asphalt road, the Bosniaks near the area had fled, the tank rolled forward and went uphill towards town. The Bosniaks who were near to Tepedzik thought it was a Croat tank. It was dark and it had passed Djurici. Our people did not react at all and the Serbs walked right into town. Their infantry realised that the support from the direction of Srt was not there. Our people realised that they were Serbs," our people being Bosniaks, I assume, "our people realised that they were Serbs and opened fire wounding and killing a certain number of their soldiers. The tank could not open fire because it was among houses and lamp posts. The Serbs picked up their dead and wounded and turned back. The infantry unit coming from the direction of the canyon was unable to climb the cliff to take position on top of the hill. They refused to surrender and turned back. The terrain was very unfavourable for an attack and when they realised they had not surprised Bosniaks, they returned." I just want to know, to have you kind of tell us what that was all about, what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a textbook attack of Serb forces against the village of Prusac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where is Djurici and where is Tepedzik?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village guarded by the Serbs or rather the line guarded by -- defended by the Serbs was in Djurici, whereas the Tepedzik settlement is located in the village of Prusac, and that was defended by the army, by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So was this -- this area, Djurici nearby Prusac?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Which was located in the Donji Vakuf municipality?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you just move up a couple of paragraphs, you speak of an attack on Prusac in August or September, 1992. You say Prusac was being constantly shelled during this period. And then you talk about marking a map of some kind. "The Serbs attacked Prusac from three directions, from Arambasisi-Radici-Srt, from Djurici-Tepedzik-Brdo and from Livopljic canyon town centre Brdo. From two of those directions they used tanks and infantry and from the last direction, only infantry." You say "they were supported by artillery, installed in the areas of Arambasici, Bozici, Vucinac, Tosicani. I was on the Bugojno front line and then I received an order from my commander to support the defence in Guvna. I was supposed to wait for HVO units and I was to take them into Prusac because they didn't know the area. They never came and I wait there in a trench. When I realised that they were not coming, I went back to Bugojno. I could see the attack because I was close to Prusac, the artillery units started shelling intensively two or three hours before the infantry attacked. The units coming from the area of Srt were stopped because the tank rolled over an antitank mine and was destroyed. The infantry which was to go forward got scared and turned back." What you're describing here is an attack by VRS forces on this village of Prusac that failed and was repulsed, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at Exhibit P1757, please. This is a document, sir, from the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior Srbobran, which is what Donji Vakuf was before they changed the name. It's dated 4 October, 1993, and the part of this report that I want refer you to is very near the end. It's the paragraph next to the last paragraph, beginning with the date on 17 August, 1992. Let me know when you've found that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It reads: "On 17 August, 1992, the operation to liberate Prusac village, which was the largest Ustasha stronghold, began at 1600 hours. Fifty-six policemen and a fair number of RS soldiers took part in the operation. After an artillery preparation, there was an infantry and tank attack from two directions. The policemen participated in these attacks and they went ahead in the first line of attack. There was hand-to-hand combat and a good part of the village was captured. By night fall, Nenad Gnjatic, a reserve policeman who was an excellent combatant, had died in combat and three policemen had been seriously wounded. Eleven soldiers died and a considerable number, around 40, were wounded. The operation was not successful because of poor command and preparation. And during the night we returned to our original positions. This was the first unsuccessful attack." So that pretty much agrees with what you told us in your statement to the Prosecutor, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The main features are that it agrees that there was artillery involved, it agrees the tanks were involved, and it agrees that infantry was involved in this attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And this was an attack by tanks and artillery and infantry on a village that you told us Friday contained a few people with a few weapons with virtually no ammunition. Is it your position that these few people with a few weapons and virtually no ammunition were able to repulse an attack by artillery, tanks and infantry?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. You gave another statement on 5 February, 2001, for the Sarajevo University Institute for the Investigation of Crimes. I'd ask the Prosecutor to make that available to you, please. I'm not sure where it is in the -- in your version but if you look at the basically the end of the document, there are two paragraphs, both beginning with the date 8 May, 1992. The paragraph before that says, "The already-complex security situation." Do you see that? It's at the end of the document, sir. Just the third --

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. The already complex security situation reached its culmination in the afternoon of 30 April, 1992, when the terrorists destroyed the bridge on the Vrbas River in the very centre of Donji Vakuf. Can you tell us who the terrorists were? And why do you call them terrorists?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for certain who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear reports that it was Croats who did that, who blew up that bridge?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Bugojno, I heard stories going around to the effect that Serbs had done it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want to talk now about a couple of entries in your diary and I need you to have your diary now. The part I want to refer to and I don't have any idea how I'm going to help you find it since we don't have it all translated, it's page 5 of the English translation, and the number is 0306-0162. And maybe the Prosecutor could help me direct you to the appropriate page in your diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would say that it is page 0207-2297 and 98.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: See if you can find 2297 and 2298, sir. 0207, it says 2292 to 2307, whatever that means. Have you found what I'm -- those pages? I'm looking for a paragraph that you wrote that begins with the language, "Open confrontation of the parties in power."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, this is in the middle of page 0207-2298.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Richterova. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Open confrontation of the parties in power resulted in increased psychosis and fear that the war might spread from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. The already-formed paramilitary national formations which are armed and as such very often threatened with war are contributing to that. Such a situation is also directly reflected --" I think maybe we should stop. Do you want to stop or do you want to go another 15 minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you but we can't stay longer than 2 or 3 minutes in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I thought we broke at 3.45, Your Honour. Am I wrong, if we start at 2.15?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "Such a situation is also directly reflected on the area of our DPZ and the voices of those who would divide villages and even municipalities or those who would attain the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the cost of war are growing louder. Those most affected by such opposing opinions are citizens of a municipality who already fear for their very lives and such a situation is worsened even more by a very low standard of living of the population." Now, that's how it was in Donji Vakuf, and you recorded it accurately, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Next page of your diary I want to talk about is -- it's 0306-0166. The page 9 of the English version. It's where you talk about only Serbs being mobilised. Do you have any idea why only Serbs would be mobilised during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is page preceding the page 0207-2305, so it is 2304 but it is not visible on that page because it's black on this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Ms. Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Why would only Serbs be mobilised? You say the mobilisation was carried out in secret and members of just one ethnic group were called up.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the mobilisation was carried out by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to -- into that in a little more detail in a little while. The next thing you write is this: You felt that such behaviour, that is mobilising only Serbs, to be extremely incorrect because as the commander of this formation said, it is possible that one ethnic group requested the protection of the JNA, so I wonder what would happen if Muslims requested protection, and then you say this: "Since I think they are just as endangered as the other inhabitants of Vakuf"; right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you agree that other inhabitants of Vakuf, that being Serbs and Croats, were also endangered?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you look at document P58, please? I'd like you to look through that document until you find Donji Vakuf, maybe it will take you long enough to do so so I can find P58.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's page 9 of original version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would be helpful if I could find the document itself but I'm having trouble doing that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no Donji Vakuf, only Srbobran here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's the one I'm tried in, and if the usher could get the English version on the ELMO so that I could look at it that way, that would solve the problem. All right. Sir, what I think you will see there are population figures from 1991 and 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in 1991, it says that the Serbs are 79.2 per cent or 12.318? You see that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I was looking at the wrong place. 1991, Serbs, 9.375, 38.7 per cent.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Muslims 13.393, 55.3 per cent?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 1995, and the usher is going to have to help me. It's probably the next page, page -- the 1995 Serbs are 8.884, 98.7 per cent; correct? Wait a minute, don't change that yet. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably is. I don't know the situation that was there on the ground in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So according to this, in 1995, there are about 500 less Serbs than there were in 1991 but now they make up 98.7 per cent of the population. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at the number of Muslims. Only 81, 0.9 per cent; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what those numbers are today, 2003? How many Serbs are living in Donji Vakuf today?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but I know that there are very few Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. We'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you. We make it 20 minutes, not 25. 20 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we go to private session for just a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, sir, we are ready again. Sorry for the little interruption. In your testimony on Friday, at page 15 of the LiveNote, line 20, you were asked this question. You were talking about checkpoints and then this question was asked of you: "And what about Muslims? Did they set up their checkpoints, let's say in Muslim villages?" Your answer was: "No they never did, they never set up a single checkpoint anywhere." Do you recall giving that answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your statement of June and September of 2001, the English is on page 8, you say this: "I found out by talking to Serbs from Donji Vakuf and from my brother-in-law who lived in Prusac, that the Bosniaks had organised a checkpoint in Prusac but I certainly wouldn't call it resistance." True?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called it a checkpoint. However, it was not really a checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what you said was that your brother-in-law told you that the Bosniaks had organised a checkpoint in Prusac. Now you're saying it wasn't really a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't look like the ones set up by Serbs because there were only two men who would stand on the road during the day and they wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you go there and look at it? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was my brother-in-law who told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And your brother-in-law told you that it was a checkpoint, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They considered it to be a checkpoint, as I have already indicated, but it was not a checkpoint -- not the kind that was usually set up by Serbs on different roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you told these Judges on Friday, with regard to the Muslims, that they never set up a single checkpoint anywhere, why did you tell the Judges that? If you're contending this wasn't really a checkpoint, why didn't you explain that to the Judges? You told the Judges on Friday that they never set up a checkpoint anywhere, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was not a single one that was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That isn't what you said Friday, is it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the checkpoints set up by Serbs on Friday. Muslims didn't have such checkpoints anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let's look at it again. The question that was asked of you: "And what about Muslims? Did they set up their checkpoints, let's say, in Muslim villages?" Now the word "armed" is not in there any where, is it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the checkpoints manned by armed people who were in charge of controlling the traffic. This is what we referred to as checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me have you answer my question. The question that was asked of you was: "And what about Muslims? Did they set up their checkpoints, let's say in Muslim villages?" The word "armed" does not appear in that question, does it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't, but that's what I imply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's clear enough now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Look at -- we got to go back to your diary again and this is always difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Richterova, if you can continue helping us --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is a table which I think you'll find at page 290 of your diary. It's 0306-0165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's easy to find.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, diary 0207-2303.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You see the table?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What does that represent? What is that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It represents the census of the population broken down per local communes of the Donji Vakuf municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the period in question was -- is before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There was a census in 1991. This would be the 1991 census, do you think?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look now at the map, P1692. Let's put it on the ELMO so that we can all look at it. Now, you see on this map that you have there, where you made a mark where this foot bridge you talked about was built. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you indicated this was a foot bridge that was built by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you told us that its purpose was to give Serbs access to Donji Vakuf without having to pass through the Muslim villages of Karici and Cehajici; right?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the Muslim settlements and local communes in Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the Serbs you're referring to were the Serbs from Brezicani?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at page 18 of the LiveNote, in your testimony on Friday, you told us - I want to make sure I get your exact words - "Then there is the village of Brezicani which is an exclusively Serb village." That was your testimony Friday; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If you look at this census table, contained in your diary, it shows that the village of Brezicani had 972 residents, of which 484 were Muslims and 425 were Serbs or that it was a majority Serb village, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this table, I was referring to local communes, not the villages. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 15047 to 15055.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've lost me. You said in your testimony that Brezicani was an exclusively Serb village. The table shows clearly --

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- that it was not, that it was mostly a Muslim village, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But Mr. Ackerman, at the top left corner of that chart or that page, you see what in English appears to be -- to have been translated "neighbourhood."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I can't imagine that makes any difference at all, Your Honour, because he didn't refer to anything but Brezicani in his testimony which he said was exclusively Serb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In his testimony he referred to it as a village and now he is telling you that what appears in this list, in his diary, is not indicated as villages but as neighbourhoods, as communes. So perhaps we'll -- not saying that what you are alleging is not correct, but I'm asking the witness to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, what's the difference between the village of Brezicani and the neighbourhood of Brezicani? What's the difference?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to explain. A local commune or a neighbourhood refers to a greater area, which consisted of several villages and hamlets. In this particular case, the local commune or the neighbourhood which was officially called Brezicani consisted of the following villages: Cehajici, Karici, Brezicani, and several other hamlets located in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So those two Muslim villages of Cehajici and Karici you're now saying were parts of Brezicani?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Brezicani local commune, not of the Brezicani village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. Now, tell me why it was that Serbs who lived in Brezicani didn't want to pass through Muslim villages on their way to Donji Vakuf? Why would that be?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will notice that very close to the village, or rather the village itself bordered the municipality of Bugojno, and it was for that reason that Serbs believed that this village was jeopardised. They could leave the village via main road leading from Brezicani towards Vrbas, along the Cehajicka River, which ran parallel with the road, and then further to this newly built bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What is the line we see on the map that goes from Brezicani below Karici and Cehajici and meets the Vrbas? What is that line?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Cehajicka River.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So one could travel from Brezicani to Donji Vakuf by going through that river and then joining the road that goes up to Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This road went parallel with the river, linking Brezicani and the Vrbas, and then downstream, along the Vrbas, up to Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you could follow that river down to the Vrbas and then follow the Vrbas into Donji Vakuf by road?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Downstream, yes, the Vrbas River.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand what difference it made to make that foot bridge. That's what I'm confused about. How did that change anything? Other than get them out of their cars and make them walk?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Donji Vakuf, on the right bank of the Vrbas River in town itself, there were two local communes. One was called Veremalija and the other one was called, I think, 27th of July. Therefore, this road went through the Veremalija local commune, which was mostly populated by Muslim residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that's all the way up in Donji Vakuf itself, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to approach it in a different manner, Mr. Ackerman, let's be practical about it. Let me ask three questions myself. Anyone who lived in Cehajici and wanted to go to Donji Vakuf, did he have a direct access road to Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had to come to the road because Cehajici and Karici are not on the road leading from Brezicani to Donji Vakuf. But they could have also gone using side roads from Cehajici, Karici and Brezicani, macadam roads. They could have used those side roads to come to Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would it have been the same applicable to those living in Brezicani?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So anyone from Brezicani who wanted to go to Donji Vakuf, would they have to pass through Karici or Cehajici or did they have other options, before the bridge was constructed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Brezicani, they had two roads they could have used to come to Karici and Cehajici and then to Donji Vakuf or they could have come down the river along the road and the right bank of the Vrbas and then pass through Veremalija local commune, and then you would get to the main and only bridge in Donji Vakuf, which was used by vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And with the construction of this bridge that you told us about last time, what would change as a result?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing changed except that the Serbs were given another option to avoid Muslim settlements, in order to reach the local commune called the 1st of May, which had a majority of Serb residents and Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough, at least in my mind, Mr. Ackerman, I don't know in yours. If it's not, you're free to ask any other question you'd like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, you just told us now that the bridge enabled them to go to something I think you called the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Enabled them to go to the 1st May, local commune, without having to pass through the other commune which was predominantly inhabited by Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I told you it's clear in my mind, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Maybe, Your Honour, but it's different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In your testimony on Friday, you said that the purpose of building the bridge was to enable the Serbs who lived in the villages of -- village of Brezicani and other neighbouring hamlets to come to Donji Vakuf without having to pass through Muslim-inhabited locations. Now you've changed the place they were going by using this bridge; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Ackerman. He said that Donji Vakuf consisted of two local communes, one is - I can't pronounce the name - which was predominantly inhabited by Muslims, Manja or whatever and the other one was the 1st May which was predominantly Serb or where a lot of Serbs lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir, is 1st May part of main town of Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town of Donji Vakuf itself consisted of four local communes, Two of which were predominantly inhabited by Muslim residents. They were called Veremalija local commune and the 27th of July. The next one was called the 16th of September. That was a mixed local commune. And then there was a local commune called the 1st of May, which also made up the downtown area of Donji Vakuf town, and that local commune was predominantly inhabited by Serb residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I guess what you're saying is by using that foot bridge, they could get to the 1st of May part of Donji Vakuf without passing through any Muslim parts of Donji Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And now I have to go back to the question I asked awe few moments ago, why would they not be willing to pass through Muslim parts of Donji Vakuf? You told us they wouldn't be willing to pass through Cehajici and Karici because they were right on the border of Bugojno municipality and they were frightened about that, but now we're talking -- you've switched to afraid to travel through Muslim parts of Donji Vakuf and I want to know why.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably planned to divide the municipality or something similar to that. I don't know why would they -- they be afraid but at any rate, throughout the time, when there was Muslim population in those local communes, Serbs always passed through the Muslim local commune and used this bridge very infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The bridge being the foot bridge?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I think we've worn that subject out. You were asked just very briefly about the term "mop up" or "mopping up" on Friday and you told us what you believed it meant. Can you tell us what is the traditional and correct military definition of that term? You described it in the context of Donji Vakuf in early 1992 but being a military man, you know the traditional and correct military definition and I'd like you to tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how is it defined in the army. I have never used that term before and I believe that there is no such term in the army. There is only a similar term used, which is search the terrain. That's the only similar military term, but as for mopping up, I've heard that this is what the Serbs did in Bosniak villages during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now a little bit about this business of mobilisation. Mobilisation was done from lists of persons who had done their basic service with the JNA and then were available in a reserve capacity to be mobilised in the event of the necessity for that. Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And these lists, I believe, were kept by -- in each municipality by the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were records there, two different kinds of records, individual ones and original, or master records, but there were no lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, who kept the lists of persons from which mobilisation would be done? It was somebody's responsibilities to maintain those lists, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Secretariat for National Defence was in charge of master records, and also in charge of personnel assigned to war units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Who was the Municipal Secretary of National Defence? Who held that position in Donji Vakuf in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Mile Ilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how long had Mile Ilic held that position?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At page 21 of LiveNote, you spoke about mobilisation and the creation of the war unit of the 19th Brigade and what you told the Judges was that this mobilisation was carried out by the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the SDS did it with the assistance of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So as far as you know, it was actually carried out properly in accordance with the law regarding mobilisation but it's your position that you think that the SDS encouraged that mobilisation, not that they actually performed it themselves?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They carried it out, implemented it and completed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: They being who, the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How did the SDS get these records that would be necessary to do the call-ups for mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The records were ignored. They carried out the mobilisation of the entire Serb population, regardless of whether they were in some other units or not, and by this I'm referring to the TO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, do you not know that there was a general mobilisation throughout the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that caused President Izetbegovic to advise Muslims not to respond to that mobilisation? You're aware of all that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if they had only been trying to mobilise Serbs, that would have been a waste of time for Izetbegovic to tell Muslims not to respond because they weren't being mobilised in the first place?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the mobilisation had started a long time before the general mobilisation in BH was declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would this be more a mobilisation that was not a mobilisation and just perhaps the creation of a paramilitary unit or something like that? Is that maybe what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look at one final document, 1754, P1754, please. I want you to look at the last page of this document, so Mr. Usher, we are actually on page -- page 4, the last three paragraphs. Now, sir, this is a document, it's a report on the work of the Donji Vakuf Public Security Station from 1 April, 1992, to 25 December, 1992. It's dated January, 1993. And signed by the chief of the SJB, Sekula Sisic. I want to refer to you the last three paragraphs of that document which read as follows: "As for explosions, fires and damage, our municipality finds itself in special circumstances since it is situated on the front line." Now, what knowledge do you have about Donji Vakuf being situated on the front line?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The demarcation line between the forces was, for the most part, the border between Donji Vakuf and Bugojno. This is where the demarcation line ran. However, the downtown area of Donji Vakuf, with the four local communes that I've mentioned was some 3 to 4 kilometres from the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. It goes on to say: "We cannot supply precise indicators, as a large number of houses and other buildings have been burned in the war operations, and practically every fortnight, the enemy shells the town and its surroundings. In this way, significant material damage is caused to buildings and the infrastructure. On 26 September, 1992, great damage was caused to the Janj DP shareholding company plant by aerial bombing. Since no record has been made of destroyed and damaged buildings, and the number is increasing day by day, we have no precise data on material damage. Finally, we would just like to mention that since 1 April, 1992, our municipality has experienced a difficult period of war operations, and we are still frequently under enemy attack." Now, Donji Vakuf, being only 3 or 4 kilometres away from the line of demarcation was, of course, within range of artillery, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And do you know, of your own knowledge, that there was artillery bombardment of Donji Vakuf along that line of demarcation, from the Bugojno side of that line?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But there was, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but very infrequently, and the data from these two parts are incorrect for the most part, and if you wish, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I don't. If the Prosecutor wants to you explain, they can ask you. I'm finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I have two issues. And I will start with the last.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If could you give us the explanation to this document and the points which are not correct in this document?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean this last segment from this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I mean this last segment.

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document makes the following claim: We are unable to give these indicators as a large number of houses and other buildings have been burned in the war operations, and so on. I can assure you that no houses were set on fire by the army shelling, nor were the facilities in the Janj compound targeted. Further on, as far as aerial bombardment is concerned, these were the planes that bombed on that day, the factory called Slavko Rodic which was located in Bugojno. That was a specialised factory, and defence factory, and a pilot who was not familiar with the municipality targeted the Janj factory in Donji Vakuf. I learned of this event from the Serbs after the war ended. We in Bugojno were very surprised to see that the Serb planes were bombing Donji Vakuf municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you said that neither of these villages was set on fire by the army shelling, so how were they set on fire?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, there wasn't a single house set on fire by the army. Almost all of them were set on fire by Serbs, who most often torched the houses of well-known and prominent Bosniaks from Donji Vakuf, as well as mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And we were talking about -- we were talking about liberation of certain villages, and you mentioned that the liberation was, among others, plundering, arson. So the arson, how did it happen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Richterova, I'm sorry about this but I need to interrupt you a minute. Let's go into private session for a while because I need to say this before 5.00, in case Mr. Ackerman needs to do something about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Again my apologies to you, Madam Richterova, and let me just repeat your question. You were told, sir, that you were asked, and we were talking about -- we were talking about liberation of certain villages, and you mentioned that the liberation was, amongst others, plundering, arson, so the arson, how did it happen? And perhaps you can answer now to that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Or better say, who did -- who set -- who set these houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what people were involved in it but I know that they were members of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was it during a combat operations?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The Defence asked you about one sentence in your statement, when you said that the SDS in Donji Vakuf, before March, 1992, received certain guidelines from higher SDS leaders regarding preparation for war, and the Defence question was, the proposition that they went there, meaning Banja Luka, to receive guidelines from higher SDS leaders, regarding preparation for war, is a conclusion that you drew based upon your knowledge they were going to Banja Luka. Did you conclude this at the time when they were going to Banja Luka or did you conclude this at the later stage? And I mean did you conclude that they were receiving certain guidelines?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that even before, before that started, so it was no secret. It wasn't just a conclusion that I drew. This was something that was publicly discussed, openly, both among the Serbs and among the Bosniaks and when we were all together in Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just to understand correctly, are you referring now to the fact that they are receiving the guidelines or the fact that they were going to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In respect of certain things that we had to agree upon, including the setup of joint checkpoints, which were supposed to be manned by Bosniaks and Serbs together, in order to designate people, this could not be done before a certain person would come back from Banja Luka and then after he would come back, then we would discuss on how to implement this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you be now specific? How did you conclude that they were receiving guidelines for preparation of war? How did you conclude this?

utterances.speaker: SENAD ALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drew this conclusion, and this was common knowledge in Donji Vakuf, especially amongst the members of the municipal administration, where these things were being discussed on a daily basis, because the municipality of Donji Vakuf had never been linked with Banja Luka. It had closer relations with Zenica. SDS officials, or Donji Vakuf municipal officials of Serb ethnicity now went to Banja Luka, which means that they were now working under the instructions coming from Banja Luka and not from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to remind the witness of his testimony on Friday, if you would permit me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Sir, on Friday, page 27, beginning at line 11, you were asked if you recall whether higher SDS leaders were going to Banja Luka to conduct some meetings or whatever, and your answer was this: "I remember they did go to Banja Luka but I don't know whether they went there for meetings or discussions or negotiations."
